story.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub

facts.text: SEOUL, June 26 (Reuters) - Samsung Group will unveil a sweeping decade-long investment plan on Monday, pledging 1,000 trillion won ($648 billion) to anchor South Korea's next growth cycle, ‌including a possible 300 trillion won push to build chip factories in the country's southwest, a media report ‌said.
Candidates across multiple regions aggressively pitched their areas as the next semiconductor hub, promising to lure giants such as ​Samsung and SK Hynix.

Presidential policy adviser Kim Yong-beom said on Wednesday that SK Hynix and Samsung may need to accelerate projects originally slated for the 2040s into the mid-2030s because AI-driven ‌memory demand was growing faster than expected, leaving no room, power ​or water in the capital region for subsequent expansion.
Electronics giant Samsung says it plans to invest around 300tn won ($230.8bn; £189.6bn) over 20 years in the South Korea government's push to develop a mega semiconductor hub in the country.
"The mega cluster will be the key base of our semiconductor ecosystem," South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said in a statement on Wednesday .
South Korea is home to other major microprocessor manufacturers such as SK Hynix.
This will be put towards building five chip factories, the firm told the BBC.
Samsung is the world's biggest maker of memory chips, smartphones and TVs.

The South Korean government has greenlit the Yongin Semiconductor National Industrial Complex three months earlier than expected, which will significantly reduce the project planning timeline, reports BusinessKorea .
The science park is said to be the world's largest semiconductor hub, accommodating multiple fabs, power plants, and fab suppliers.
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware.
In-depth features, interviews and insider stories from the world of hardware.
Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor.
To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea.
Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online.
Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air.

And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips.
It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex.
Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers.
They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards.
Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park.
They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments.
Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes .
